Issued at 330 AM EDT Wed Oct 14 2026

===== Anticipating Isolated Flash Flooding Threat Today and Warm=====

Now in the early overnight, the CWA is going through another quiet 
period well ahead of a trough that has dug itself deep over the 
southern Plains into the Texas panhandle. With the aid of strong 
moisture transport at the surface and all the way up to 700mb, there 
is plenty of juice for potential showers and storms to rely on to 
produce heavy downpours. 

Currently, storms have fired off near central Missouri and seem to 
be on track to arrive in our CWA by late morning to the early 
afternoon hours hitting our southern Indiana counties first in a SW-
NE oriented line. PWATs will be increasing ahead of the storms 
reaching near or just over 2.00" which is at all but the 100th 
percentile of climatology. Instability will increase ahead of the 
line of storms with modeled MUCAPE reaching near 1,500 J/kg in some 
areas by this afternoon. However, the best shear will remain too far 
north of our area, along with less than favorable jet dynamics to 
further support lift as these storm progress eastwards towards 
central and later eastern KY. That being said, these storms should 
be fairly progressive despite the amount of juice in the atmosphere. 
Additionally, at this time, it appears should there be another wave 
of storms late this evening that the primary wave should produce 
more rain than any subsequent wave. All this to say it appears the 
flash flood threat will be mostly limited to this first round of 
rain and it remains to be seen how much additional rain will fall 
beyond that.

Looking upstream, personal weather stations have been reporting at 
most 2-3". Even here, there is better forcing for lift without at 
least widespread reports of over 4" or so. Knowing this, rainfall 
totals should vary from location to location, with 25th-75th 
percentile total precipitation estimates from HREF data ranging 
about 0.25-1". Short range models are struggling to ascertain how 
the somewhat limited instability and storms diverging from the best 
support will evolve over KY, hence the rather large spread in 
rainfall totals (HREF values of total precipitation is currently 
left skewed to under 0.5"). 

These storms out in Missouri are tending to grow in vertical height, 
collapse under their own weight, and gust out a surface boundary 
that chokes out the next line of storms too far into the cold pool 
while acting as an axis of convective activity for cells further 
south rising into and above the boundary. There's currently a 
boundary situated west-to-east just south of St. Louis that may 
focus the next incoming round of storms. Should the next round now 
in central Missouri hold together without collapsing first, it would 
affect most of our CWA by late morning/early afternoon. 6hr LPMM 
data from HREF indicate isolated areas of 2-5" are possible by 
Wednesday evening after that first line passes through. The biggest 
concern for any flash flooding according to the latest 6hr FFG would 
be southern Indiana counties, a south-north oriented stripe of 
communities from Hart to Trimble counties (from rainfall from 
Isaias), and the Bluegrass region NE of Lexington. Strong to severe 
gusty winds are possible with these storms as well, should they 
continue to build up and collapse, though the larger concern remains 
isolated flash flooding.

Highs today range in the upper 70s across southern Indiana (who will 
be the first to cloud over from convective debris and incoming 
storms) to the mid and upper 80s near Lake Cumberland. High 
forecasts are tricky today and will solely depend on the speed and 
prevalence of storms. A strong high temperature gradient may exist 
between NW and SE areas as a result.

The boundary responsible for the storms today will stall somewhere 
over our area by evening, most likely close to the TN. Communities 
north of this line will remain on the cool side versus warm and 
continuous SW flow south of this line. Moisture will stay locked in 
overnight, and with calming winds and remnant chances of showers 
riding along the boundary from west to east, widespread fog is 
likely to form at least north of the boundary.

=====Lingering Showers and Warm Thursday=====

Beginning Thursday morning, another developing low will move across 
the central Plains near Iowa and move towards Great Lakes region, 
helping to strengthen a return to SW flow in the afternoon. This in 
turn will lift our aforementioned boundary as a warm front through 
the Ohio Valley and a return to summery heat --again, this late in 
October! The center of the low and continuous moist flow from the 
Gulf may be close enough to spawn additional showers in the morning
